tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Do not set `run_in_background=true`; background task management tools are not available.

**Commands available:**
The following common command categories are usually available. Availability still depends on the host, so when in doubt run `which <command>` first to confirm a command exists before relying on it.
- Navigation and inspection: `ls`, `pwd`, `cd`, `stat`, `file`, `du`, `df`, `tree`
- File and directory management: `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `ln`, `chmod`, `chown`
- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`
- Archives and compression: `tar`, `gzip`, `gunzip`, `zip`, `unzip`
- Networking and transfer: `curl`, `wget`, `ping`, `ssh`, `scp`
- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

1	# richgo
2	
3	Rich-Go will enrich `go test` outputs with text decorations.
4	
5	[![asciicast](https://asciinema.org/a/99810.png)](https://asciinema.org/a/99810)
6	
7	## Description
8	
9	richgo is a command-line tool that adds color and formatting to the output of Go's `go test` command, making test results easier to read and understand.
10	
11	## Installation
12	
13	### Using go get
14	
15	```
16	go get -u github.com/kyoh86/richgo
17	```
18	
19	### Using homebrew
20	
21	```
22	brew install kyoh86/tap/richgo
23	```
24	
25	### Using asdf
26	
27	```
28	asdf plugin add richgo
29	asdf install richgo 0.3.6
30	```
31	
32	## Usage
33	
34	### Basic Usage
35	
36	```sh
37	richgo test ./...
38	```
39	
40	### In an existing pipeline
41	
42	If your build scripts expect to interact with the standard output format of `go test` (for instance, if you're using [go-junit-report](https://github.com/jstemmer/go-junit-report)), you'll need to use the `testfilter` subcommand of `richgo`.
43	
44	For example:
45	
46	```sh
47	go test ./... | tee >(richgo testfilter) | go-junit-report
48	```
49	
50	This will "tee" the output of the standard `go test` run into a `richgo testfilter` process as well as passing the original output to `go-junit-report`.
51	
52	### Creating an alias
53	
54	You can define an alias so that `go test` prints rich outputs:
55	
56	* bash: `~/.bashrc`
57	* zsh: `~/.zshrc`
58	
59	```
60	alias go=richgo
61	```
62	
63	## Configuration
64	
65	### Configuration file paths
66	
67	It's possible to change styles with a preference file. Rich-Go loads preferences from the files in the following order:
68	
69	* `${CWD}/.richstyle`
70	* `${CWD}/.richstyle.yaml`
71	* `${CWD}/.richstyle.yml`
72	* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle`
73	* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle.yaml`
74	* `${GOPATH}/.richstyle.yml`
75	* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle`
76	* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle.yaml`
77	* `${GOROOT}/.richstyle.yml`
78	* `${HOME}/.richstyle`
79	* `${HOME}/.richstyle.yaml`
80	* `${HOME}/.richstyle.yml`
81	
82	Setting the environment variable `RICHGO_LOCAL` to 1, Rich-Go loads only `${CWD}/.richstyle*`.
83	
84	### Configuration file format
85	
86	Rich-Go supports YAML formatted configuration files.
87	
88	```yaml
89	# Type of the label that notes a kind of each lines.
90	labelType: (long | short | none)
91	
92	# Style of "Build" lines.
93	buildStyle:
94	  # Hide lines
95	  hide: (true | false)

98	  faint: (true | false)

100	  underline: (true | false)
101	  blinkSlow: (true | false)
102	  blinkRapid: (true | false)

104	  inverse: (true | false)
105	  conceal: (true | false)
106	  crossOut: (true | false)
107	  frame: (true | false)
108	  encircle: (true | false)

112	  # Back-color of text
113	  background: # Same format as `foreground`
114	
115	# Style of the "Start" lines.

118	
119	# Style of the "Pass" lines.

121	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
122	
123	# Style of the "Fail" lines.

125	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
126

129	  # Same format as `buildStyle`
130

132	fileStyle:

134

149

151	coveredStyle:

163	```
164	
165	### Line categories
166	
167	Rich-Go separates the output lines into the following categories:
168	
169	* **Build**: Build error messages
170	* **Start**: Test start lines (e.g., `=== RUN   TestSampleOK/SubtestOK`)
171	* **Pass**: Test pass lines (e.g., `--- PASS: TestSampleOK/SubtestOK`)
172	* **Fail**: Test failure lines (e.g., `--- FAIL: TestSampleNG (0.00s)`)
173	* **Skip**: Test skip lines (e.g., `--- SKIP: TestSampleSkip (0.00s)`)
174	* **PassPackage**: Package pass indicator (`PASS`)
175	* **FailPackage**: Package fail indicator (`FAIL`)
176	* **Cover**: Coverage analysis lines
177	
178	Each category can be styled separately.
179	
180	### Label types
181	
182	* **Long**: BUILD, START, PASS, FAIL, SKIP, COVER
183	* **Short**: !!, >, o, x, -, %
184	* **None**: Rich-Go will never output labels.
185	
186	### Default configuration
187	
188	```yaml
189	labelType: long
190	buildStyle:
191	  bold: true
192	  foreground: yellow
193	startStyle:
194	  foreground: lightBlack
195	passStyle:
196	  foreground: green
197	failStyle:
198	  bold: true
199	  foreground: red
200	skipStyle:
201	  foreground: lightBlack
202	passPackageStyle:
203	  foreground: green
204	  hide: true
205	failPackageStyle:
206	  bold: true
207	  foreground: red
208	  hide: true
209	coverThreshold: 50
210	coveredStyle:
211	  foreground: green
212	uncoveredStyle:
213	  bold: true
214	  foreground: yellow
215	fileStyle:
216	  foreground: cyan
217	lineStyle:
218	  foreground: magenta
219	```

221	### Solarized Dark theme compatibility
222	
223	The bright-black is used for background color in Solarized dark theme. Richgo uses that color for "startStyle" and "skipStyle", so "START" and "SKIP" lines may not be visible on screens with Solarized dark theme.
224	
225	To resolve that conflict, you can set another color for "startStyle" and "skipStyle" in your `.richstyle` file:
226	
227	```yaml
228	startStyle:
229	  foreground: yellow
230	
231	skipStyle:
232	  foreground: lightYellow
233	```
234	
235	## Overriding colorization detection
236	
237	By default, `richgo` determines whether or not to colorize its output based on whether it's connected to a TTY or not. This works for most use cases, but may not behave as expected if you use `richgo` in a pipeline of commands.

239	To force colorization, add `RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR=1` to the environment:
240	
241	```sh
242	RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR=1 richgo test ./... | tee test.log
243	```
244	
245	## Getting the version
246	
247	If you want to get the version of `richgo`, this information is embedded in the binary (since Go 1.18). You can view it with `go version -m`:

253		mod	github.com/kyoh86/richgo	v0.3.10	h1:iSGvcjhtQN2IVrBDhPk0if0R/RMQnCN1E/9OyAW4UUs=
254		[...]

261	v0.3.10
262	```

part.text:
# DOMAIN 6 Behavioral Spec: `test` subcommand, delegation, exit codes, TTY detection

Environment used: go1.21.0 linux/amd64, temp module `example.com/probe` with `passpkg` (TestAdd pass, TestSkip skip), `failpkg` (TestFail fails), `builderr` (syntax error), `GOPROXY=off GOFLAGS=-mod=mod`.

## 1. Command dispatch

- `richgo test ...` → runs `go test ...` with **args passed through verbatim** (no `-v` or any flag added/removed/reordered). Evidence: `richgo test -count=1 ./passpkg/` non-color stdout is byte-identical to `go test -count=1 ./passpkg/` (modulo trailing-newline quirk below); `-run`, `-v`, `-json` all honored; `richgo test --help` is byte-identical to `go test --help` (usage on **stderr**, exit **2**).
- `richgo testfilter [any extra args ignored]` → reads stdin, writes filtered stdout. Extra args (`testfilter foo bar`) silently ignored, exit 0. Never touches `go` (works with empty PATH).
- Any other first arg (`version`, `env GOPATH`, `build`, `frobnicate`, no args) → delegated to `go` with direct stream attachment (no filtering/styling ever), byte-identical output, exit code propagated:
  - `richgo version` → `go version go1.21.0 linux/amd64\n`, exit 0.
  - `richgo frobnicate` → stderr `go frobnicate: unknown command\nRun 'go help' for usage.\n`, exit **2** (same as `go frobnicate`).
  - `richgo` (no args) → go usage text on stderr (1804 bytes), exit **2**.
- `go` is located via **PATH lookup** (a symlink `go` in a custom PATH dir works). If `go` is not in PATH, richgo **panics** (exit **2**):
  - delegated cmd: stdout empty, stderr = `panic: exec: "go": executable file not found in $PATH\n\ngoroutine 1 [running]:\nmain.main()\n\t/workspace/main.go:74 +0x465\n`
  - `test`: stdout = `\n`, stderr = `\n` + same panic text (both filter streams emit their EOF newline first).

## 2. Colorize decision — keyed on **stderr**, not stdout (quirk!)

Colorization is ON iff `RICHGO_FORCE_COLOR` env var is **set to any non-empty string** (`1`, `0`, `false`, `garbage`, `TRUE`, `2` all enable; empty string and unset do not) **OR fd 2 (stderr) is a TTY** (real isatty check: `/dev/null` does not trigger). `NO_COLOR` and `TERM=dumb` are ignored.

Verified asymmetry (no force var):
- `richgo test`/`testfilter` with stdout=file, **stderr=PTY** → output written to the file is **fully styled with ANSI escapes**.
- stdout=PTY, **stderr=file** → output on the PTY is **plain** (non-color mode).

The decision is global: when on, BOTH the stdout-filter and stderr-filter of `richgo test` style their content; when off, both pass through.

## 3. `richgo test` plumbing

Runs `go test` with stdout→filter→richgo's stdout and stderr→filter→richgo's stderr (build errors, which `go test` writes to stderr, are styled in color mode: `ESC[33mESC[1mBUILD| example.com/probe/builderr\nESC[0m...`).

Exit code = go test's exit code exactly: pass→0, test failure→1, build error→1, `test --help`→2, bad usage→1/2 as go does.

**Trailing-newline quirk (deterministic, verified with 2s-slow tests):**
- go test **succeeds** (exit 0): each filter, in **non-color mode only**, appends exactly one extra `\n` at EOF. So stdout = go's stdout + `\n`; stderr (usually empty from go) = `\n`. Example: `richgo test -count=1 ./passpkg/` (stdout & stderr split, non-color) → stdout `ok  \texample.com/probe/passpkg\t0.002s\n\n`, stderr `\n`, exit 0. In color mode: no extra bytes (`ESC[32mPASS  | example.com/probe/passpkg ESC[0m\n`, stderr empty).
- go test **fails** (exit≠0): the extra EOF newline is **suppressed on both streams** — stdout/stderr are exactly the filter output with no trailing addition (non-color: byte-identical to `go test`; color: styled, hidden lines removed).

## 4. Filter behavior (applies to `testfilter` and `richgo test`'s pipe)

Non-color mode = **byte-for-byte pass-through of every line** (no hiding, no labels, `=== RUN`/`PASS`/`FAIL` all verbatim), with this EOF rule: every input line is terminated (a final unterminated line gets `\n` appended); then, iff input was empty or ended with `\n`, one extra `\n` is written. Verified: `''`→`\n`; `hello`→`hello\n`; `hello\n`→`hello\n\n`; `\n`→`\n\n`; `hello\nworld\n`→`hello\nworld\n\n`.

Color mode (representative exact bytes, default styles):
- `ok  \tfoo\t0.1s\n` → `ESC[32mPASS  | foo ESC[0m\n` (timing replaced by single trailing space; standalone `PASS` line hidden entirely — `hide:true`)
- `FAIL\texample.com/probe/failpkg\t0.002s\n` → `ESC[31mESC[1mFAIL  | \texample.com/probe/failpkg\t0.002sESC[0m\n`; standalone `FAIL` lines hidden
- `=== RUN   TestAdd\n` → `ESC[90mSTART| AddESC[0m\n` (`Test` prefix stripped)
- `--- PASS: TestAdd (0.00s)\n` → `ESC[32mPASS  | Add (0.00s)ESC[0m\n`
- test log line `    pass_test.go:12: skipping\n` → `ESC[90m     |     ESC[36mpass_test.goESC[0mESC[35m:12ESC[0mESC[90m: skippingESC[0m\n` (blank 5-space label + `| `; file cyan, `:12` magenta)
- uncategorized lines (e.g. `-json` output) → prefixed with blank label `     | ` (5 spaces, pipe, space), no escapes
- `testfilter` exit code is **always 0**, even for `FAIL` input.

## 5. Notes for the implementer

- The panic on missing `go` (message text + exit code 2) should be reproduced; the goroutine trace path/offset (`/workspace/main.go:74 +0x465`) is build-specific.
- The stderr-based TTY check looks like an upstream bug but is 100% deterministic — reproduce it exactly (isatty on fd 2).
- The "extra `\n` on success only" behavior of `richgo test` suggests: filter EOF-finalization runs only when exit code is 0; on failure richgo exits without it. In color mode the EOF newline never happens.
- Config files (`.richstyle*`) were not created anywhere; `/workspace` untouched; all temp dirs cleaned up.
